course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 9

unit.title: Interpreting and discussing results
unit.blurb: Frequency polygons, scatter graphs and correlation, back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagrams, statistics for grouped data and choosing good representations.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Draw and interpret frequency polygons, including comparing two distributions.

O2.t: Draw and interpret scatter graphs, describe correlation and use a line of best fit.

O3.t: Use back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagrams to compare two sets of data (median and range).

O4.t: Estimate the mean, and find the modal class and the class containing the median, for grouped data.

O5.t: Choose and criticise representations of data, and draw conclusions from them.

p: If there is correlation, draw a **line of best fit**: a straight line through the middle of the points, with roughly equal numbers of points either side (it doesn't have to go through the origin).

p: A reviewer tests 40 phones and groups their battery life (hours) into classes. She has lost the individual results.
Can she still find an average? How accurate will it be? Think about it before you read on.
Mean = Σ(value × frequency) ÷ Σ frequency.
With grouped data we don't know the exact values, so use each **class midpoint** as an estimate:
**Modal class**: the class with the highest frequency → 15 ≤ t < 20.

**Median class**: the class containing the middle value. 40 values → the 20th and 21st: running totals 6, 20, 32 … → the 20th is in 15 ≤ t < 20, the 21st in 20 ≤ t < 25 – so the median is around 20 h.
**Estimated range**: largest possible − smallest possible = 30 − 10 = 20 h (an upper estimate).

captions: A school nurse has five sets of data: favourite sports, students' heights, height against arm span, reaction times for two year groups, and sick days each month.
She must choose a chart for each.
Height against arm span: a scatter graph, or a Venn diagram?
Pause the video and choose.
A scatter graph, because each student gives two measurements, and we want to see if they are related.
Remember the charts you know: bar, pie, line, frequency diagrams and polygons, scatter graphs, stem-and-leaf, Venn and Carroll diagrams.
Match the chart to the data and the question.
Continuous data for one group: a frequency diagram.
Comparing two groups: frequency polygons, or back-to-back stem-and-leaf.
Change over time: a time series graph.
Your turn.
Favourite sports: a bar or pie chart, or a scatter graph?
Pause the video and choose.
A bar chart or a pie chart.
Sports are categories.
Justify your choice.
For example: a time series graph, because I want to show how sick days change from month to month.
Here is the method.
Step 1: what type of data is it: categories, numbers, or pairs?
Step 2: what is the question: proportion, trend, relationship, or comparison?
Step 3: choose the chart, and justify it.
Step 4: check it is clear and honest: labels, scales, a key.
A pie chart of hours of sleep uses the groups 6 or more, 7 or more, 8 or more and 9 or more.
The groups overlap, so one person is counted in several slices.
Your turn.
Overlapping categories in a pie chart are: misleading, or fine?
Pause and choose.
Misleading.
The slices must not overlap.
Use separate groups, and a bar chart or frequency diagram.
A bar chart of attendance whose axis starts at 90 makes 92 and 95 percent look very different.
Start at 0, or show a break.
The nurse wants to show how sick days changed each month.
Ana chooses a chart.
Which line is wrong?
Line 1 is wrong.
A pie chart hides the order of the months.
Use a time series graph to show the trend.
Public health posters, news graphics and company reports all depend on clear, honest charts.
One last question.
To compare two classes' marks and keep the exact values: back-to-back stem-and-leaf, or pie charts?
Pause the video and choose.
A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram.
It keeps every value, and puts the two classes side by side.
To remember: match the chart to the data and the question.
Scatter for relationships, time series for trends, polygons or back-to-back for comparing.
Justify your choice.
Spot misleading features.
Great work! Now practise lesson 15.5 on Camday.
